Why I Stopped Reaching for a Framework First

Posted by J. Okonkwo on 12 March 2026

MARKER_BLOG_LEDE For most of the last decade my answer to "we need a web page" started with npm install. Not because the problem demanded it, but because the toolchain had become muscle memory: scaffold, pick a router, configure a bundler, fight the type checker, ship a hundred kilobytes of JavaScript to render what is, at the end of the day, a document.

The turning point was a weekend project that needed a changelog page. I caught myself pricing out a component library for what was literally a list of dated paragraphs. So I wrote the HTML by hand, spent twenty minutes on a stylesheet, and deployed a single file. It loaded instantly, it survived being archived, and it cost me an afternoon instead of a toolchain.

None of this is an argument that frameworks are useless. A multi-user dashboard with live updates earns its dependencies. The mistake is letting the biggest hammer in the box define what a nail looks like. A marketing page, a blog, a changelog, a documentation set — these are documents first, and the browser already knows how to render documents.

The fastest code is the code that never ships to the client.

The practical discipline I ended up with is embarrassingly simple: start with a static file. When a real interaction requirement appears — not an imagined one, a filed ticket or a user complaint — add exactly the mechanism that requirement needs and nothing more. A sprinkle of vanilla script covers an astonishing amount of ground.

<details>
  <summary>No JavaScript required</summary>
  Disclosure widgets are native now.
</details>

There is a maintenance dividend too. The static pages I shipped five years ago still render identically today. The framework apps from the same era have all been through two migrations and a bundler funeral. Dependencies are a mortgage; sometimes the house is worth it, but the payments never stop.

  • Documents want HTML and CSS, not a runtime.
  • Interactions want the smallest mechanism that fits.
  • Frameworks want a justification, not a default.

Your mileage will vary with the problem, and mine is only one data point. But the next time a page-shaped problem comes along, it is worth asking whether the browser alone might already be the framework you were about to install.
